intrinsic_value_estimate: $70-125 per share, central estimate about $100. Method: value to a private owner, built on owner earnings (brk-letter-1986). 1988 owner earnings are about $2.60/share: net income $1,044.7M + D&A $169.8M + deferred taxes $43.9M - undistributed equity income $35.8M - capex somewhere between depreciation and the full $386.8M, less preferred dividends, on 364.6M average shares. These are discounted at about 9% (an assumed government bond yield; the packet has none). Owner earnings grow 8-15% a year for 10 years (the 1981-88 record is about 12%), then 4% a year. Stress test at management's 12% cost of capital: $45-60. The literal net-working-capital test (bpl-letter-1965) gives $1.06/share NWC and fails; it applies to bargain generals, not to an outstanding business bought at a sensible price (brk-letter-1987#18).
margin_of_safety: At $46.56: about 54% below the $100 central value; 32-37% in the conservative cases (8% growth, or zero growth after year 10); about 22% at a 12% discount rate with 12% growth. The margin disappears only if a 12% discount rate is combined with growth below about 8.5%. The price implies only about 2% annual owner-earnings growth at a 9% discount rate. The framework sets no fixed percentage; for a high-confidence franchise it asks for a 'sensible price' with a real margin (brk-letter-1981#3, brk-letter-1987#18), and this price clears that.

key_reasons.reason: Passes every gatekeeper: not a turnaround, does not need debt to operate, simple, consistent earning power, management in place, large enough to matter.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 2. Filters / gatekeepers (turnarounds seldom turn; avoid businesses that need debt) and 1. Berkshire acquisition criteria
key_reasons.evidence: EPS rose every year from $0.84 (1977) to $2.85 (1988). Operating cash flow $1,167M vs capex $387M in 1988. Management calls soft drinks a 'low capital requirement' business with 'high return on investment' (ar-1988). Market value $16.5B.

key_reasons.reason: Exceptional return on equity, earned before any leverage and still high once leverage and the affiliates are stripped out.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (without undue leverage or accounting gimmickry)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE 21-23% in 1978-81 with debt/capital under 10%. In 1988, about 24% on net capital (unlevered); the core, excluding about $2.07B of affiliates earning 2.5%, earns about 42% after tax; soft drink operating income $1,690.7M on $3,809M of identifiable assets.

key_reasons.reason: A durable, widening moat built on trademark and distribution, with pricing power and a long runway.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle
key_reasons.evidence: World share up from under 38% (1981) to nearly 45% (1988), more than double the next competitor; US fountain share 59%; 63% gross margin on concentrate (ar-1986); Latin America operating income +17% on +1% volume; servings per person per year 51 internationally vs 274 in the US; daily servings 359M to 559M over 1981-88.

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings and backed by cash.
key_reasons.evidence: 1988: before-capex figure $1,222.6M; after full capex $835.8M; with maintenance assumed equal to depreciation, $1,052.8M. Estimate $2.45-2.75/share vs reported $2.85. Operating cash flow $1,167M vs net income $1,045M.

key_reasons.reason: Management has turned retained earnings into far more market value and repurchases shares at prices well below value.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value; buybacks only well below intrinsic value
key_reasons.evidence: 1981-88: about $6.46/share retained vs +$33.50 price gain, about $5.20 per $1 (about $2.60 at a constant P/E). Repurchased 18.4M/15.0M/2.9M/14.2M/19.0M shares in 1984-88 at about 12-18x EPS; average shares fell from 396M to 365M; 14.4M shares still authorized.

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible against private-owner value, with a large margin of safety.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 5. Valuation, as applied to an outstanding business at a sensible price (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 = 16.3x 1988 EPS, about 5.6% owner-earnings yield, plus about 7.5% of market value returned each year (2.9% dividend at the $1.36 rate, 4.6% buyback); central value about $100; implied growth about 2% at a 9% discount rate.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst needed; the price lagged the business after others turned fearful.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 6. No catalyst needed: the market eventually reflects business results; 9. Be fearful when others are greedy
key_reasons.evidence: Price $50.56 in Aug 1987 (about 21x) vs $46.56 now (16.3x) while EPS rose 17%; 1988 range $35-45 after the October 1987 crash.

key_reasons.reason: Concentrate heavily, but below the 40% maximum because owner-earnings inputs and currency are uncertain.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 7. Concentrate when the facts are clear (up to 40% of net worth)
key_reasons.evidence: Maintenance capex not disclosed; 76% of operating income from outside the US with a 10% weaker dollar in 1988; net debt about 24% of capital. The resulting position, roughly $0.8-1B on an assumed $3-4B net worth (not in the packet), is about 5-6% of the company.

risks: A stronger dollar: about 76% of operating income is earned outside the US, and 1986-88 benefited from 27%/16%/10% currency gains.
Maintenance capital spending is not disclosed; the low case ($2.27/share owner earnings) cuts value by about 13%.
Management-chosen leverage: total debt/capital 38.8%, net-debt ceiling raised to 35%, buybacks partly debt-funded.
About $1.9B sits in bottler and entertainment affiliates earning 2.5-6%; the CPE write-down of $114M shows the risk of diversification.
Rising advertising ($648M to $842M, 1986-88) is needed to defend the moat; bottler economics may limit concentrate price increases.
Hyperinflation and political instability in Latin America (Argentina and Brazil volumes fell in 1988).
Stock option grants jumped to 4.18M in 1988; a restricted-stock change-of-control clause was added.
The discount rate is assumed: the packet has no government bond yield, and at a 12% rate combined with growth below about 8.5% the margin disappears.
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that maintenance capex is near total capex and owner earnings are well below $2.30/share.
Constant-currency results showing the 1985-88 growth came mostly from exchange rates rather than volume and price.
Meeting management reveals weak integrity, low insider ownership, or continuing ambitions to diversify outside soft drinks.
Long-term government bond yields well above 10%, which would make the 12% stress test the base case.
Data showing a narrowing gap with the primary competitor in key markets, or falling concentrate margins per case.
sell_triggers: Lasting erosion of the moat: sustained loss of world or US share, or concentrate margins falling and not recovering.
Management redirecting retained earnings into large unrelated acquisitions, or issuing shares for less value than it receives (brk-letter-1982#17).
Leverage beyond the self-imposed 35% net-debt ceiling for reasons other than buybacks well below value, especially if needed to sustain operations.
Evidence of misleading reporting by management (failure of candor, brk-letter-1983#2).

Default is to hold permanently (brk-letter-1987#18); a higher price alone is not a trigger. Selling would be considered only at an extreme, sustained valuation far above any reasonable owner-earnings value, with a clearly better use of the capital.
